title: How to work around pain
summary: Part one of a series prompted by a viewer named Pedro. NH says never lift through pain; instead swap or lighten the offending lift. He illustrates with a recent low-back cramp during squats at 365 lb: he stopped the set, switched to front squats, cut back-squat reps to 4 the following sessions, used paused squats at 300 lb, and kept deadlifting because he knows the issue is his SI joint, not deadlift-related.

claims.claim: Never lift through pain; if a movement hurts, stop doing it. Pushing through turns minor issues into critical, possibly lifelong ones.

Two weeks earlier NH squatted 365 lb for 6 without trouble, then felt a left low-back cramp on rep 3 of the next set of 5; he racked the bar immediately, didn't retry, stripped the bar and switched to front squats.
At 22-23 he pushed through pain and got seriously injured; handled properly, a small pinch or cramp is gone soon and costs no strength or size.
Front squats deload the back, so they are a good substitute when back squats aggravate the lower back.
The next squat session he did 365 lb for only 4 instead of pushing for 6-7, then front squats, then paused squats at 300 lb for 4, where the cramp appeared on the right side.
He reasoned the right-side cramp came from favouring the right side because the left was hurt, overtaxing it.
The following session he did 365 lb x4, front squats, and paused squats at 300 lb for 4,4,4 with no pain: he worked around the pain while keeping leg volume.
He kept deadlifting (about 425 lb for 4) because he knows his squat back pain comes from a weak SI joint and doesn't affect his deadlift; this relies on deep knowledge of his own body.
If a lift aggravates some pain, change it: back squat hurts, try front squats; heavy back squat hurts, try lighter. There is always a way around for every lift.
NH distinguishes being 'hurt' from being 'injured' and plans videos on the difference.
